emperor-tenmu.name: Emperor Tenmu
emperor-tenmu.summary: 40th emperor of Japan (c. 630–686), who took the throne after winning the Jinshin War against his nephew and modeled his government on Tang China.

soga-clan.name: Soga clan
soga-clan.summary: A powerful aristocratic family of early Japan's Asuka period who helped spread Buddhism and dominated the imperial court's succession and policy in the 5th–7th centuries.

asuka-period.name: Asuka period
asuka-period.summary: Period in Japanese history lasting from 538 to 710 CE, named after the Asuka region, marked by the arrival of Buddhism and adoption of Chinese writing that transformed Japanese society.

empress-k-ken.name: Empress Kōken
empress-k-ken.summary: Japan's 46th and 48th monarch, who reigned first from 749 to 758 and again later as Empress Shōtoku, navigating court factions and a close alliance with the monk Dōkyō.

empress-gensh.name: Empress Genshō
empress-gensh.summary: 44th monarch of Japan, reigning from 715 to 724, and the only Japanese empress to inherit her title from another reigning empress rather than a male predecessor.

emperor-sh-mu.name: Emperor Shōmu
emperor-sh-mu.summary: 45th emperor of Japan, reigning from 724 to 749 during the Nara period.

nihon-shoki.name: Nihon Shoki
nihon-shoki.summary: The second-oldest book of classical Japanese history, completed in 720, giving the most complete surviving record of ancient Japan from myth through the 8th century.

kagoshima-prefecture.name: Kagoshima Prefecture
kagoshima-prefecture.summary: Prefecture on Japan's island of Kyushu that formed the core of the Satsuma Domain, an important domain of the Edo period and Meiji Restoration.

mi-province.name: Ōmi Province
mi-province.summary: A former province of Japan matching modern Shiga Prefecture, centered on Lake Biwa, Japan's largest lake, and ranked among the empire's 13 'great countries.'

gandhara.name: Gandhara
gandhara.summary: An ancient Indo-Aryan region centered on the Peshawar valley, in what is now northwest Pakistan and northeast Afghanistan, known as an influential Buddhist civilization.

greco-buddhist-art.name: Greco-Buddhist art
greco-buddhist-art.summary: Also called Gandhara art, a style blending Ancient Greek and Buddhist art that flowered under the Kushan Empire and produced the first known depictions of the Buddha in human form.

three-kingdoms-of-korea.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
three-kingdoms-of-korea.summary: The era when the Korean peninsula was divided among the rival kingdoms of Goguryeo, Paekche and Silla, whose peoples became the Korean people.

paekche.name: Baekje
paekche.summary: A Korean kingdom in southwestern Korea from 18 BCE to 660 CE, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, notable as a maritime power that spread Buddhism to Japan.

goguryeo.name: Goguryeo
goguryeo.summary: Korean kingdom (37 BC–668 AD) covering much of the Korean peninsula and parts of Manchuria, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea and the source of the name Korea.

taedong-river.name: Taedong River
taedong-river.summary: A major North Korean river flowing through Pyongyang into Korea Bay, near which many ancient painted tomb murals have been found.

mireuksa.name: Mireuksa
mireuksa.summary: The largest Buddhist temple of the ancient Korean kingdom of Baekje, founded in 602 by King Mu near modern Iksan and home to one of Korea's oldest pagodas.

iksan.name: Iksan
iksan.summary: A South Korean city and rail junction in North Jeolla Province, nicknamed 'the City of Jewelry,' formed when the town of Iri merged with Iksan County in 1995.

takamatsuzuka-tomb.name: Takamatsuzuka Tomb
takamatsuzuka-tomb.summary: A circular burial mound from Japan's Asuka period, located in Nara and designated a National Historic Site in 1972.

ch-g-ji.name: Chūgū-ji
ch-g-ji.summary: A Buddhist nunnery founded in the 7th century by Shōtoku Taishi in Nara Prefecture, Japan, home to a Miroku statue and Tenjukoku mandala that are National Treasures.

prince-sh-toku.name: Prince Shōtoku
prince-sh-toku.summary: A semi-legendary regent of Japan's Asuka period who served under Empress Suiko, renowned for modernizing government administration and promoting Buddhism.

maitreya.name: Maitreya
maitreya.summary: Bodhisattva regarded in Buddhism as the future Buddha, prophesied to succeed Gautama Buddha and re-establish his teachings on Earth.

k-ry-ji.name: Kōryū-ji
k-ry-ji.summary: A Shingon Buddhist temple in Kyoto, said to be the city's oldest, founded in 603 after Hata no Kawakatsu received a Buddhist statue from Prince Shōtoku.

yakushi-ji.name: Yakushi-ji
yakushi-ji.summary: An ancient imperial Buddhist temple in Nara, Japan, originally built in the 7th century and rebuilt in 730, headquarters of the Hossō school of Buddhism.

s-ryaprabha.name: Sūryaprabha (Nikko)
s-ryaprabha.summary: A bodhisattva associated with sunlight and good health, known in Japanese as Nikko, often paired with Candraprabha (Gakko) as attendants of the healing Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru.

candraprabha.name: Gakko (Candraprabha)
candraprabha.summary: A bodhisattva of moonlight who, with his sibling Suryaprabha, serves the healing Buddha Bhaisajyaguru; the two are often shown flanking temple doors.

mur-ji.name: Murō-ji
mur-ji.summary: Shingon Buddhist temple in Nara Prefecture, Japan, home to one of the oldest surviving five-storied pagodas, built in the 9th century.

shingon-buddhism.name: Shingon Buddhism
shingon-buddhism.summary: A major school of Japanese Esoteric Buddhism founded by the monk Kūkai (774–835) after he studied in Tang China, centered at Mount Kōya.

battle-of-mount-jupil.name: Battle of Mount Jupil
battle-of-mount-jupil.summary: An 11 July 645 AD battle in which Tang Chinese forces wiped out a Goguryeo relief force sent to defend the fortress city of Ansi.

silla.name: Silla
silla.summary: A Korean kingdom lasting from 57 BCE to 935 CE, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, which eventually conquered the other two and unified much of the peninsula.

unified-silla.name: Unified Silla
unified-silla.summary: Period of the Korean kingdom of Silla after it conquered Goguryeo in 668 CE, unifying the central and southern Korean peninsula until it fell to Goryeo in 935.

parhae.name: Balhae
parhae.summary: A multiethnic kingdom founded in 698 by Tae Choyŏng, spanning Northeast China, the northern Korean Peninsula, and the Russian Far East until conquered by the Liao dynasty in 926.

battle-of-baekgang.name: Battle of Baekgang
battle-of-baekgang.summary: A 663 AD battle in which allied Silla and Tang China forces decisively defeated Paekche restoration forces and their Japanese Yamato allies, ending Japan's involvement in Korean affairs.

later-three-kingdoms.name: Later Three Kingdoms
later-three-kingdoms.summary: A period of early medieval Korea, from around the 890s to 936 AD, marking a partial revival of the ancient Three Kingdoms.

emperor-taizong-of-tang.name: Emperor Taizong of Tang
emperor-taizong-of-tang.summary: Second emperor of China's Tang dynasty (598–649), regarded as one of China's greatest rulers; his reign, the Zhenguan era, is considered a golden age of Chinese history.

yeongnyu-of-goguryeo.name: Yeongnyu of Goguryeo
yeongnyu-of-goguryeo.summary: The 27th monarch of Goguryeo, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, who reigned from 618 until his death in 642.

y-n-kaesomun.name: Yŏn Kaesomun
y-n-kaesomun.summary: Powerful military dictator of the late Goguryeo kingdom (594–666) whose resistance against Tang China made him a hero to some, though traditional histories cast him as a despot.

ky-n-hw-n.name: Kyŏn Hwŏn
ky-n-hw-n.summary: King and founder of Later Baekje, one of Korea's Later Three Kingdoms, who ruled from 892 to 935.

gwangju.name: Gwangju
gwangju.summary: A South Korean city, formerly capital of South Jeolla Province and once the country's sixth-largest metropolis, merged into a new provincial city in 2026.

later-paekche.name: Later Paekche
later-paekche.summary: A Korean kingdom founded in 900 by the Silla general Kyŏn Hwŏn, reviving the old Paekche identity in Jeolla Province before falling to Goryeo in 936.

jeonju.name: Jeonju
jeonju.summary: The capital and largest city of South Korea's Jeonbuk state, with over 1,300 years of history, known for Korean cuisine, historic buildings and festivals.

goryeo.name: Goryeo
goryeo.summary: Korean kingdom founded in 918 that unified the peninsula and ruled until 1392, giving Korea its name and becoming a golden age of Buddhism and commerce.

liaodong-peninsula.name: Liaodong
liaodong-peninsula.summary: A peninsula and historic region in Northeast China east of the Liao River, whose name comes from an ancient commandery and which was long contested by Chinese and Korean powers.

gyeongsun-of-silla.name: Gyeongsun of Silla
gyeongsun-of-silla.summary: Last ruler (897–978) and 56th monarch of the Korean kingdom of Silla.

kojiki.name: Kojiki
kojiki.summary: An early Japanese chronicle of myths, legends and genealogies compiled around 711–712, considered the oldest surviving literary work in Japan and a foundation of Shinto tradition.

man-y-sh.name: Man'yōshū
man-y-sh.summary: The oldest surviving collection of Japanese poetry, compiled after 759 CE, gathering more than 4,500 poems written by people ranging from emperors to soldiers and peasants.

nara-period.name: Nara period
nara-period.summary: A period in Japanese history from 710 to 794, when the capital was established at Heijō-kyō (modern Nara) and Japan's upper classes adopted Chinese writing, fashion and Buddhist schools.

man-y-gana.name: Man'yōgana
man-y-gana.summary: An ancient Japanese writing system, in use by at least the mid-7th century, that used Chinese characters purely for their sounds to spell out Japanese words, later giving rise to hiragana and katakana.

kana.name: Kana
kana.summary: Japanese syllabic writing systems, chiefly hiragana and katakana, in which each character represents a phoneme or syllable rather than a whole word.

heian-period.name: Heian period
heian-period.summary: The last division of classical Japanese history (794–1185), a peak of imperial court art and literature even though real power lay with the Fujiwara clan.

hyangga.name: Hyangga
hyangga.summary: Poems written with Chinese characters during Korea's Unified Silla and early Goryeo periods; only a few dozen survive.

tanka.name: Tanka
tanka.summary: Genre of classical Japanese short poetry and one of the major genres of Japanese literature.

kanshi-poetry.name: Kanshi
kanshi-poetry.summary: A Japanese term for Chinese poetry in general, and for poetry written in Chinese by Japanese poets, most popular among aristocrats in the early Heian period.

bussokuseki-kahi.name: Bussokusekika
bussokuseki-kahi.summary: A set of 21 poems inscribed on a Buddha-footprint monument built in 753 CE at Yakushi Temple in Nara, an early form of Japanese waka poetry.

kakinomoto-no-hitomaro.name: Kakinomoto no Hitomaro
kakinomoto-no-hitomaro.summary: A Japanese waka poet and aristocrat (c. 653–710) considered the most prominent poet in the Man'yōshū anthology, remembered for elegies to imperial princes and later revered as a god of poetry.

princess-nukata.name: Princess Nukata
princess-nukata.summary: A Japanese poet of the Asuka period, daughter of Prince Kagami, who became Emperor Tenmu's favorite wife and bore him a daughter.

waka-poetry.name: Waka (poetry)
waka-poetry.summary: A form of poetry in classical Japanese literature, also called yamato-uta, distinct from the Chinese-style kanshi verse.

urashima-tar.name: Urashima Tarō
urashima-tar.summary: The protagonist of a Japanese fairy tale about a fisherman carried to an undersea palace, who returns home to find a hundred years have passed, based on 8th-century legends.

kokin-wakash.name: Kokinshū
kokin-wakash.summary: An imperial anthology of Japanese waka poetry conceived by Emperor Uda and published around 905 under Emperor Daigo, compiled by four court poets led by Ki no Tsurayuki.

the-tale-of-the-bamboo-cutter.name: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
the-tale-of-the-bamboo-cutter.summary: A late 9th- or early 10th-century Japanese folk tale, the oldest surviving work of its form, about Kaguya-hime, a princess from the Moon found as a baby inside a glowing bamboo stalk, who later returns there.
the-tale-of-the-bamboo-cutter.source_title: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter

samguk-yusa.name: Samguk yusa
samguk-yusa.summary: A collection of Korean legends and historical accounts compiled by the Buddhist monk Il-yeon around 1280; it holds the earliest surviving record of the Dangun founding legend.

cheomseongdae.name: Cheomseongdae
cheomseongdae.summary: The oldest surviving astronomical observatory in Asia, built in Gyeongju, Korea, during the reign of Queen Seondeok of Silla (r. 632 to 647 CE); it is a UNESCO-listed national treasure.

kaya-confederacy.name: Kaya confederacy
kaya-confederacy.summary: A confederacy of small Korean city-states in the Nakdong River basin, traditionally dated 42 to 532 CE, later absorbed by Silla.

toraijin.name: Toraijin
toraijin.summary: Ancient people who migrated to Japan (and their naturalized descendants), who introduced Confucianism, Buddhism, Chinese writing, medicine and other practices, mainly from the 4th to 7th centuries.

ishinp.name: Ishinpō
ishinp.summary: The oldest surviving Japanese medical text, completed in 984 by Tamba Yasuyori in 30 volumes, drawing on Chinese medicine and preserving otherwise-lost Chinese sources.

taejo-of-goryeo.name: Wang Kŏn (Taejo of Goryeo)
taejo-of-goryeo.summary: Founder of Korea's Goryeo Dynasty, ruling from 918 to 943, who achieved unification of the Later Three Kingdoms in 936.

kung-ye.name: Kung Ye
kung-ye.summary: King of the short-lived state of Taebong (901–918) during Korea's Later Three Kingdoms period, claimed to be a son of a Silla king, who became a rebel leader against Silla's government.

bone-rank-system.name: Bone-rank system
bone-rank-system.summary: The hereditary system of aristocratic rank in the ancient Korean kingdom of Silla, dividing society by closeness of bloodline to the throne.

taika-reform.name: Taika Reform
taika-reform.summary: A set of doctrines established by Emperor Kōtoku in 645 that centralized Japan's imperial government, modeled on Confucian ideas and Tang Chinese administration.

samhan.name: Samhan
samhan.summary: The collective name for three confederacies—Byeonhan, Jinhan and Mahan—that arose in southern Korea in the 1st century BCE and later developed into the Baekje and Silla kingdoms and the Kaya confederacy.

heij-ky.name: Heijō-kyō
heij-ky.summary: Japan's capital during most of the Nara period (710–784), modeled on Tang China's Chang'an, which grew into an international hub of up to 100,000 people.

chang-an.name: Chang'an
chang-an.summary: Capital of several Chinese dynasties, including the Western Han and Tang, from 202 BCE to 907 CE, and at times the largest city in the world; known today as Xi'an.

nagaoka-ky.name: Nagaoka-kyō
nagaoka-ky.summary: The capital of Japan from 784 to 794, located in what is now the Kyoto area, before the court moved on to Heian-kyō.

heian-ky.name: Heian-kyō
heian-ky.summary: The imperial capital of Japan established in 794 in what is now Kyoto, modeled on China's Chang'an, remaining the seat of the Imperial Court for most of the following millennium.

fujiwara-clan.name: Fujiwara clan
fujiwara-clan.summary: A powerful family of imperial regents in Japan that dominated the imperial court, especially through intermarriage, from ancient times until the Meiji Restoration in 1868.

liao-dynasty.name: Liao dynasty
liao-dynasty.summary: A Khitan-led imperial dynasty of China (916–1125) that at its height ruled Manchuria, Mongolia, northern Korea, and parts of Siberia and North China.

mohe-people.name: Mohe
mohe-people.summary: Historical Tungusic-speaking peoples of Northeast Asia during late antiquity, a major population of the kingdom of Balhae, and ancestors of the later Jurchen and Manchu peoples.

mononobe-clan.name: Mononobe clan
mononobe-clan.summary: A Japanese noble clan of the Kofun period that served as court armorers and opposed the spread of Buddhism, clashing with the pro-Buddhist Soga clan.

mikky.name: Mikkyō
mikky.summary: Japanese Esoteric Buddhism, a lineage of Vajrayana Buddhism brought to Japan mainly by the monk Kūkai in the early Heian period, involving complex icons, meditative rituals and ritual languages.

kofun-period.name: Kofun period
kofun-period.summary: An era in Japanese history from about 300 to 538 AD, marked by Chinese and Korean cultural influence and thousands of large burial mounds, ending with Buddhism's introduction.

kami.name: Kami
kami.summary: Deities, spirits, and natural or ancestral forces venerated in Japan's traditional Shinto religion, seen as part of nature rather than separate from it.

shinbutsu-sh-g.name: Shinbutsu-shūgō
shinbutsu-sh-g.summary: The historical syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism in Japan, in which kami worship and Buddhism became closely intertwined from the 6th century until their formal separation in 1868.

empress-suiko.name: Empress Suiko
empress-suiko.summary: 33rd monarch of Japan and the country's first reigning empress, ruling from 593 to 628.

t-dai-ji.name: Tōdai-ji
t-dai-ji.summary: Buddhist temple complex in Nara, Japan, founded in 738 CE and opened in 752, home to the world's largest bronze Buddha statue and headquarters of the Kegon school of Buddhism.

daibutsu.name: Daibutsu
daibutsu.summary: The Japanese term for a giant statue of Buddha; the oldest dates to 609, and the best known is at Tōdai-ji in Nara, completed in 752.

k-kai.name: Kūkai
k-kai.summary: A Japanese Buddhist monk, calligrapher and poet (774–835) who studied esoteric Buddhism in China and founded Japan's Shingon school on his return.

saich.name: Saichō
saich.summary: A Japanese Buddhist monk (767-822) who founded the Tendai school after studying in Tang China in 804, establishing its headquarters at Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei near Kyoto.

tendai.name: Tendai
tendai.summary: A Mahayana Buddhist school founded in Japan in 806 by the monk Saicho, based on Mount Hiei, that became a dominant Buddhist tradition by the Kamakura period.

lotus-sutra.name: Lotus Sutra
lotus-sutra.summary: One of the most influential Mahāyāna Buddhist scriptures, teaching that all Buddhist paths lead to Buddhahood; it founded the Tiantai school and later Tendai and Nichiren traditions.

tiantai.name: Tiantai
tiantai.summary: An East Asian school of Mahayana Buddhism that developed in 6th-century China, centered on the Lotus Sutra and chiefly founded by Zhiyi.

mount-hiei.name: Mount Hiei
mount-hiei.summary: Mountain near Kyoto, Japan, site of the Enryaku-ji temple founded in 788 that became the center of the Tendai Buddhist sect.

jianzhen.name: Jianzhen
jianzhen.summary: Tang-dynasty Chinese Buddhist monk (688–763) who, after several failed attempts, finally reached Japan in 753, losing his eyesight along the way, and founded Tōshōdai-ji temple in Nara.

yayoi-period.name: Yayoi period
yayoi-period.summary: A period of Japanese history (about 300 BC to AD 300) marked by the shift to wet-rice farming and new pottery, following the Jomon period and preceding the Kofun period.

kamado.name: Kamado
kamado.summary: A traditional Japanese wood- or charcoal-fueled cook stove.

william-wayne-farris.name: William Wayne Farris
william-wayne-farris.summary: American historian of premodern Japan (born 1951), focused on social, economic and demographic history.

gofuku.name: Gofuku
gofuku.summary: Japanese word for kimono fabrics and other cloth or dry goods, originally meaning clothing woven in the style of the Wu Kingdom in China.

wu-region.name: Wu region
wu-region.summary: A region of China centred on Lake Tai, south of the Yangtze River, named after historical kingdoms once based there.

hiragana.name: Hiragana
hiragana.summary: A Japanese phonetic syllabary, alongside katakana and kanji, that developed from cursive simplifications of Chinese characters via man'yōgana and is used for grammar, particles and native words.

katakana.name: Katakana
katakana.summary: One of Japan's kana syllabaries, used mainly for foreign loanwords, emphasis and technical terms, its characters derived from fragments of more complex kanji by Buddhist monks.

kanji.name: Kanji
kanji.summary: Chinese characters adapted for writing Japanese, used since ancient times alongside the phonetic hiragana and katakana scripts.

samguk-sagi.name: Samguk sagi
samguk-sagi.summary: A history of Korea's Three Kingdoms completed in 1145 under King Injong of Goryeo; it is the oldest surviving Korean chronicle, compiled by the official Kim Pusik.
